Sorry for wall of text, but it is the whole story.

Arthur L. Smith III was a familiar figure around his Madison Township neighborhood.

An auto mechanic for 30 years before health issues sidelined him, Smith often could be found walking with his personal cart, full of groceries or sometimes scrap metal. He would walk through his neighborhood off Noe-Bixby Road or to the nearby commercial strip along Hamilton Road, where the city of Columbus cuts into the township along Route 33 in southeastern Franklin County.

It's a route that Smith, 61, was walking on Feb. 26, a sunny, 40-degree afternoon and a welcome respite from a cold winter.

Get the news delivered to your inbox: Sign up for our morning, afternoon and evening newsletters

A few miles away, a 2001 Chevrolet Cruze blew by Lt. Edward Schillig of the Franklin County sheriff's office on Route 33 just west of the Fairfield County line, initially clocked at 88 mph. The lieutenant pulled out to pursue the eastbound car, intending to cite the driver for excessive speed.

He soon would learn that driver Ramadhan H. Muridi and four other Michigan youths — all of them 12 to 16 years old — had been on their way to Florida in the car, which was reported stolen five days earlier. Inside were about a dozen stolen credit cards to help fund their trip, plus a credit-card skimmer.

The pursuit lasted 10 minutes, but by the end, it would be tragically intertwined with Smith's daily routine, and it would change the lives of all involved.

The details of the high-pressure, high-speed chase are documented in the dash-cam video from Schillig's cruiser, radio communications and investigative records.

Schillig, a 21-year veteran and a supervisor able to decide for himself the terms of a pursuit, sees the Cruze is not going to stop for him. The car belongs to a Lansing, Michigan, woman who had left her purse, with a spare car key inside, in her unlocked car on Feb. 21.

Now her Cruze is speeding into Fairfield County. Twice, the car swerves onto the median berm, flying past other cars as if they were parked. As the Cruze approaches the traffic signal at the Pickerington Road interchange, the driver makes a risky U-turn from a left-turn lane just before Pickerington Road.

"He made a U-turn and almost hit me," Schillig tells the dispatcher.

As the vehicles head west, back into Franklin County, the speed and intensity pick up. The Chevy veers onto the median and right shoulder berms. Schillig, still in pursuit, tells the dispatcher four times that the Cruze's estimated speed is 110 mph.

A deputy sheriff throws stop sticks onto the highway just south of the Gender Road exit, hoping to flatten the car's tires, but misses the Cruze.

A few minutes later, the Cruze comes up on slowing and stopped traffic on westbound? Route 33. The car veers to the right berm, speeding past stopped vehicles at it approaches the Hamilton Road exit. A box truck moves over to the berm, blocking the Cruze's path, so the car is forced to swerve back onto the road.

Another deputy is right there, waiting with stop sticks along Route 33.

"He got spikes," the deputy radios.

Two of the four tires on the Cruze are punctured. The car darts off the highway and heads north on Hamilton Road, near the area where Smith is walking with his cart.

Schillig follows and attempts to do a "pit" maneuver, in which his cruiser would tap the Cruze's back bumper to spin it sideways, but with no success.

The Cruze, which Schillig reports is traveling north on Hamilton Road at about 60 mph, accelerates into oncoming traffic in the southbound lanes with the sheriff's office SUV in pursuit.

Just north of the Hamilton Square shopping center, Smith is walking across Hamilton Road between vehicles that have stopped for him because there is no crosswalk or traffic light

"Oh, crap," Schillig says as he sees the car approach Smith.

Smith is almost across the road when the Cruze strikes him with its right front side, sending him flying into the air and breaking the passenger-side front windshield.

"He just hit someone! He just hit someone!" Schillig yells. "He hit a human!"

The Chevy then drives erratically onto a grassy area off the west side of Hamilton, returns to the southbound lanes and weaves through traffic into the northbound lanes and turns east on Winchester Pike. The Cruze drives across several front lawns before coming to a stop in the front yard of a home in the 4600 block of Winchester Pike at 2:26 p.m.

Smith's 29-year-old son, Anthony, learned what happened to his father through a cellphone call from a neighbor who had seen the elder Smith's cart on Hamilton Road. When Anthony couldn't reach his father by phone, he drove to Hamilton Road.

"I walked over and asked the sheriff's deputy if the cart belonged to my dad. If it's my dad's cart, I need to know," Anthony said. The deputy walked away, and when he returned, he told Anthony that his father was in stable condition.

Anthony says that he immediately knew it was much worse. "He didn't take his cart."

For the next three months, Anthony spent nearly every day at OhioHealth Grant Medical Center. His father, whom he described as "extremely helpful and friendly to everyone," never regained consciousness. He died on May 25, two days after being removed from life support.

Captured

The five young occupants scramble out of the Chevy as soon as it stops. As they do, Schillig's SUV turns into the front yard and bumps into the front fender. When Schillig sees the car's driver with the red hoodie running toward the rear of the property, he drives after him, passing two of the passengers until a small wall forces him to stop and get out of the SUV.

Schillig runs after the driver, yelling, "Stop or I'll kill you!"

The suspect continues to run, but minutes later, he and the four passengers — two boys and two girls — are in custody as other deputies swarm the area.

A search of the stolen Cruze reveals a strong odor of alcohol and several empty bottles, prompting a search warrant to draw blood from the driver.

The test finds that Muridi, 16, was impaired from marijuana. He is charged with a delinquency count of vehicular homicide.

On Tuesday, Muridi appeared in Franklin County Juvenile Court for a hearing. The Franklin County prosecutor is asking that Muridi be tried as an adult. Muridi has a record of juvenile offenses in Michigan, the sheriff's office said. Judge Kim Browne set another hearing for Aug. 26 to review the issue.

Meanwhile, the cases of the four passengers have gone through Juvenile Court. All were found guilty of delinquency counts of receiving stolen property, and three of them were found to have obstructed official business. They were put on probation for a year, ordered to do 24 hours of community service, fined $100 and returned to Michigan.

Reprimand

After the chase, Schillig was issued a written reprimand for his conduct in the pursuit.

The reprimand cites the sheriff's office's pursuit policy and notes that Schillig drove on both the median and right shoulder berms at speeds near 100 mph. The reprimand states that Schillig had the responsibility to "continually weigh all factors that are relevant to the safety of the public."

"He was reprimanded because he erred in judgment," Chief Deputy Jim Gilbert told The Dispatch. Schillig's initial decision to pursue was within policy, Gilbert said, but "when traffic became heavy after Gender Road, due to speeds and traffic, we believe he should have terminated it at that point."

Schillig disagrees and is appealing. He did not return a phone call seeking comment.

The 45-year-old lieutenant has received a number of commendations during his career, records show.

The reprimand is one issue, but Gilbert said there is no question who is responsible for Smith's death: "Ultimately, this pursuit started based on the suspect's actions while operating the vehicle. (Muridi's) actions were very reckless that day."

Anthony Smith attended Tuesday's hearing in juvenile court and declined comment afterward. He did share some thoughts in an earlier interview.

"Where does forgiveness still apply?" Anthony wonders aloud. "Is it to be forgiven because they're kids? Where are the parents?"
